South Korea's 2017 presidential elections are about to take place. Two major political parties and their leaders have been fighting for the presidency: the conservative incumbent Saenuri and the liberal New Politics Alliance for Democracy (NPAD). The front runners in the race are Moon Jae-in of the NPAD and former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki Moon running for Saenuri.

Moon Jae-in, defeated by Park Geun-hye in the 2012 election, has again campaigned on a primarily liberal platform while promising to bolster national security by increasing military spending in order to advance the power of the South Korean military. The end goal of this strategy is for the Republic of Korea to take total control of its defense networks instead of relying on US support.

Ban Ki Moon has ran on a center-right platform with more focus on diplomacy, which plays towards the former UN leader's strengths as a diplomat and experiences in his former position. While focusing more on diplomacy, recent world events have seen Ban Ki Moon also move towards supporting a strengthening of South Korea's military.

The South Korean people have chosen Moon Jae-in as their next President. Pundits believe that Ban Ki Moon's advanced age of 73 played a part in his defeat. Moon Jae-in will assume office on the 25th of February.

ELI5: Why do we need both eyes to perceive depth?

Draw a line. Now without knowing the length of the line and only knowing the position of one end show me with math how long it is.

Or draw 3 lines in a triangle. You know the length of one line and the degree of the angles at both ends. Find the length of the other lines with math.

Parallax is a displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight, and is measured by the angle or semi-angle of inclination between those two lines.

Pretty much saying each eye sees an object from a different angle. As you view the object with one eye, you can see it move relative with the background based on each eye's line of sight. The difference in movement lets your determine the distance in which said object is from you.

And your brain is so awesome you just become accustomed to figuring out the distance thanks to parallax without thinking about it. It becomes second nature. Like throwing a ball. Or washing a dish, for the other half of you.
Hell, accurately throwing stuff is a minor miracle in itself.

Throwing is hard. In order to deliver a baseball to a batter, a pitcher has to release the ball at exactly the right point in the throw. A timing error of half a millisecond in either direction is enough to cause the ball to miss the strike zone.

To put that in perspective, it takes about five milliseconds for the fastest nerve impulse to travel the length of the arm.[6] That means that when your arm is still rotating toward the correct position, the signal to release the ball is already at your wrist. In terms of timing, this is like a drummer dropping a drumstick from the 10th story and hitting a drum on the ground on the correct beat.

This is really difficult to ELI5, especially since your brain does most of the "heavy lifting" in a way that's difficult to explain... but let's try.

With only one eye, you only get one "image." This image, like a picture or move, can only be processed as an image. There's only so much "information" you can only get so much from a single, linear image. Linearly, you can only see that something is in front of another thing, but that's all of the information you can get.

But, when you add a second image, which you can superimpose onto the first, you can see the changes between the two images. Your brain takes these "changes" and calculates the depth by comparing each and every piece in both.

Imagine a room with stuff against all of the walls, and with a table in the middle of it. When you look at the table with your right eye, it'll be in front of certain objects... but when you look at it with your left eye, it'll be in front of different objects. Your brain takes this "crossing" of the two images (with the table at the intersection of the X) and automatically determines how far the table and the objects behind it are using how "different" the two images are.

The more different they are, the further away these items appear to each other... the less different they are, the closer the items appear to each other... but this doesn't tell us how far objects are from us, just how far away they are from each other. We (our brains) discretely do this for everything around us, determining how far away our feet are from our heads, then how far away the floor is from our feet, and how much floor is between us and that table... This is what we determine as depth perception.

It's also how we make 3D movies and pictures with specialized glasses... this is called a stereogram (stereo = two; gram = picture). The transparent glasses are polarized in opposite ways, so that one eye only sees image #1, and the other eye only sees image #2... and red/blue glasses filter out images so the red lens can only see the blue image, and the blue lens can only see the red image.

In the image/movie, there are literally two images projected at the same time. Depending on how "far apart" the same line is from its red/blue counterpart, it'll look closer or farther away. Our brains, again, compare this with the wall/screen the image is "projected" on, on which the lines are literally the same for both eyes, and our brains see this as a "standard" for everything else to project into or out of. Just like the table in our example intersects at the X, the wall would be at the focal point of that same X, leaving the rest of the image to be in an area of more or less deviation.

While this answer is indeed long, I think the first few paragraphs are the simplest and best response to the question.

Cool fact: owls have offset ears which allow them to hear in 3D much in the same way we see. Their ears are on either side of their skull, like our eyes are, and they also have a high and low ear giving them up/down directional hearing. This allows them to hunt, in flight, in a 0 lumen environment - truly complete darkness!

ELI5: Why are we our own worst critics?

Sticking with looks say someone has a small mole on their other wise flawless face. Everyday they get up and they see their face, nothing special they have seen this face nearly every day of their lives, BUT GODDAMMIT THERE IS A FUCKING MOLE IN THE MIDDLE.

Now they go about their day and meet someone else. The other person sees someone who is astonishingly beautiful, they probably don't even notice the mole.

Never underestimate the mind's ability to torture itself, and everyone has had plenty of time for their minds to accumulate all sorts of ammunition to use on such occasions.

To boil it down, it is not that the person who thinks they are ugly, are seeing themselves in the mirror as they are, and saying they are ugly. What they are really seeing is their reflection, coupled with all the negative associations their mind has established over the years.

All that emotional baggage, all those memories of when people have said mean spirited things about them, or situations where they have suffered a blow to their ego, or been told they are inadequate. All those things get piled on top of the reflection, until they sink in like some poorly administered fake tan and become incorporated into their body image.

They don't just see the reflection of the person, they see their self worth, and in their mind, they are ugly, worthless, socially inept wastes of space.

Some people end up having plastic surgery to fix what they deem to be wrong, never realising that what they are trying to fix is not physical and cannot be tucked, nipped, or clipped away.
